VGGT First-Frame Invariance Probe

R2Dreamer L1 · 2M-step checkpoint (step 2000000) · HM3D house fK2vEV32Lag.basis.glb · two protocols: navigate (139 matched frame pairs) and teleport (150 matched frame pairs)

At the same physical viewpoint reached from two different starts — in teleport the very same camera pose, so the RGB input image is identical — the raw VGGT World-Points the world model ingests are essentially unrelated (cosine -0.00) and the encoder embedding cosine is only 0.31. The only thing that changed is which frame VGGT took as its first-frame reference. It propagates downstream: the trained model's belief diverges by JS 0.44 nats (63% of maximum; memory cosine 0.62), identically under both protocols. The 2M-step world model is not invariant to the start pose — the first-frame-relative encoding flows straight into its latent state.
Method note. Every number and figure below is computed directly from what the VGGT pipeline emits (raw World-Points, Camera-Pose, the encoder embedding) and from the Dreamer RSSM latents. No rigid or scale alignment is applied anywhere — alignment is not part of the pipeline, so it is not part of the test. We compare the representations exactly as the model produces and consumes them. The shared pipeline is documented in architecture-data-flow.html.

1 · What we did

VGGT turns each RGB frame into World Points (WP, 37×37×3) and a Camera Pose (CP, 9-d) expressed relative to the first frame of its streaming window; the Dreamer encoder consumes the flattened 4116-d WP‖CP vector. For the canonical WP/CP route into replay, the encoder, and the RSSM, see the global architecture/data-flow reference. If the encoding were invariant, the same physical state would map to the same representation regardless of where the episode started. We test this with two protocols (5 start poses in one house, ≈30 frames each), each comparing a forward pass with a backward pass that revisits the same places in a fresh VGGT window:

  • navigate the agent physically walks back — same positions, but the camera faces the opposite way (realistic; heading also changes, so the RGB differs too).
  • teleport the agent is placed at the exact forward poses (same position and heading) in reverse, so the RGB image is identical. Only the first-frame reference differs — the clean test.

2 · What we found

3 · How to read the numbers

  • Cosine (raw WP, embedding, memory): 1 = identical direction, 0 = unrelated, <0 = opposed. Raw 3-D coordinates of the same room in two first-frames are rotated/translated, so their cosine sits near 0 even though the scene is identical — and this is the actual vector the model ingests.
  • Why embedding cosine (0.31) > raw WP cosine (-0.00)? The encoder is a single learned linear map W·x + b. The bias contributes little; the weight W projects onto directions that partly overlap across frames — so it leaks a bit less, but a linear layer cannot undo a start-dependent rotation, so it stays far below 1.
  • Belief JS (nats): distance between the two posterior belief distributions. 0 = same belief, ln2 ≈ 0.69 = no overlap. Our 0.44 ≈ 63% of max ⇒ the model thinks it is in a substantially different situation at the same spot.
  • Memory cosine (deter): similarity of the 2048-d recurrent state. 0.62 ⇒ partially aligned, far from identical.
  • Navigate vs teleport. In navigate the camera also faces the other way, so the RGB and the frame differ; in teleport the RGB is identical and only the first-frame reference differs. The belief JS is essentially the same in both (0.44 → 0.44) — so the non-invariance is not an artefact of the heading change, it is the first-frame reference itself.

4 · Is this actually a problem? — pro & against

▲ Pro — a real problem

  • No stable world anchor in the input. The same state maps to WP with cosine ≈ 0 depending on the arbitrary start frame — even when the RGB image is byte-for-byte identical (teleport).
  • It reaches the belief state. JS ≈ 0.44 nats (63% of max), memory cosine 0.62: the latent is not a function of physical state alone — against the world-model premise.
  • Robust, not an artefact. Essentially identical under navigate and teleport, so it is not the heading confound.
  • Likely hurts cross-start generalization and any representation reuse across episodes.

▼ Against — may not matter / fixable

  • Same scene, moving origin. The WP are not corrupted, only re-expressed relative to a different first frame — the geometric information is present, so an expressive model could in principle learn a frame-invariant feature.
  • Within an episode the reference is fixed, so the representation is perfectly stable for within-episode control — all ObjectNav deployment needs.
  • The task only needs relative geometry ("goal relative to me now"), which is preserved.
  • Our belief metric is cross-episode; the model never matches latents across episodes at deploy, so the gap may overstate task-relevant harm.
  • Magnitude is moderate — memory cosine 0.62 is well above unrelated.

5 · Takeaway

The first-frame-relative property of VGGT is real and propagates into the world model's latent — a concern for cross-start generalization and representation reuse, though it is an information-preserving frame ambiguity (the same room re-expressed in a moving origin) and is benign for within-episode control. Open question for the thesis: does anchoring WP/CP to a world / gravity-aligned frame (or a learned canonicalization) inside the pipeline improve transfer across start poses? The metrics here — raw-WP cosine, encoder-embedding cosine, belief JS — are the yardstick to test it.
